Pipkin the squirrel was beside himself with delight. He had just discovered the most magnificent oak tree he had ever seen, its branches heavy with ripe, plump acorns. He chattered excitedly to Bartholomew the badger, who was dozing near his burrow entrance.

"Oh, Bartholomew!" cried Pipkin. "You simply must see it! The biggest oak in all the woods, just across the Whispering Brook! I shall be the fattest squirrel this winter!"

Bartholomew slowly opened one eye. "The Whispering Brook, you say?" he rumbled, a deep tremor in his voice. "It has been raining these past few days, little one. The brook can be a tricky friend when its temper is up."

"Nonsense!" Pipkin chirped, already turning to dart away. "I am nimble and quick. A few wet stones are nothing to me!"

"Wet stones," Bartholomew mused, "can be as slippery as ice. And the current, too, runs strong after a good shower. It might just whisk a careless squirrel off his feet."

Pipkin, however, was far too eager to heed the full measure of Bartholomew's warning. His mind was already filled with the crisp taste of fresh acorns. He scampered to the edge of the brook, his tail twitching with anticipation. The water indeed looked swifter than usual, and the stepping stones were dark and gleaming with moisture. "Just a quick hop," he told himself, "and then to the feast!" He sprang onto the first stone, then the second. But the third was slicker than he had imagined. His tiny paws lost their grip. With a surprised yelp, he tumbled sideways. One paw dipped into the icy, rushing water. He scrabbled desperately, his heart pounding like a drum, barely managing to claw his way back to the bank, soaked and shivering.

A moment later, Bartholomew emerged from the undergrowth, shaking his head. "I told you so, didn't I, my young friend?" he said, his voice softer now. "The brook takes no heed of a squirrel's hunger; it has its own schedule."

"I... I nearly fell in!" Pipkin stammered, his fur plastered flat. "It was much harder than I thought."

"Indeed," Bartholomew replied. "Always respect the water, Pipkin. Now, if you truly wish for those acorns, there is a fallen log half a mile upstream. It is a longer journey, but a much safer one, especially when the brook is in such a mood."

Pipkin looked sheepish, his earlier pride quite forgotten. "Thank you, Bartholomew," he said. "I am glad you were here. I would have been quite lost if you... ." He paused, shaking his head. "I guess even a nimble squirrel can learn a thing or two from a wise old badger."

Bartholomew merely smiled, a slow, knowing smile. "Experience," he declared, "is a good teacher. And sometimes, a cold dunking is the quickest lesson of all." He then turned and amled towards the path, Pipkin following close behind, his grand plans for a swift crossing thoroughly dampened.
